C001.fun_fact: A honeybee must visit roughly two million flowers to make a single pound of honey, pollinating your garden all the while.

C002.fun_fact: Monarchs migrate thousands of miles to Mexico, but no single butterfly makes the whole round trip—it takes several generations.

C003.fun_fact: A single convergent ladybug can eat thousands of aphids in its lifetime, making it a gardener's tiny pest-control ally.

C004.fun_fact: The Big Dipper firefly males flash a distinctive J-shaped swoop of light on warm summer evenings to attract a mate.

C005.fun_fact: Green lacewing larvae are such fierce aphid hunters they're nicknamed 'aphid lions.'

C006.fun_fact: Earthworms tunnel through soil eating their way along, and their castings enrich garden beds with nutrients plants love.

C007.fun_fact: A ruby-throated hummingbird's wings beat about 50 times a second, letting it hover and even fly backward at your flowers.

C008.fun_fact: The common green darner is one of the few dragonflies that migrates, with generations relaying south and north each year.

C009.fun_fact: Female eastern tiger swallowtails come in two color forms—the familiar yellow and a dark form that mimics the toxic pipevine swallowtail.

C010.fun_fact: Eastern cottontails don't dig their own burrows; they rest in shallow grass nests called forms, often right at the garden's edge.

C011.fun_fact: Northern cardinals don't migrate and keep their brilliant red all winter, glowing against New England snow.

C012.fun_fact: Black-capped chickadees hide thousands of seeds each fall and can remember where they stashed them months later.

C013.fun_fact: American robins don't smell worms—they cock their heads to watch and listen for them moving in the soil.

C014.fun_fact: Eastern bluebirds readily nest in garden boxes and feast on the insects and grubs that trouble your plants.

C015.fun_fact: An eastern chipmunk can stuff its cheek pouches with food until they swell to the size of its head before scurrying home.

C016.fun_fact: Red squirrels are fiercely territorial and famously noisy, scolding intruders—including gardeners—with loud chatter.

C017.fun_fact: Gray treefrogs can change color from gray to green to match their perch, and they survive winter by partly freezing solid.

C018.fun_fact: Eastern garter snakes are harmless garden helpers that eat slugs, grubs, and other pests among your plants.

C019.fun_fact: A white-tailed deer flashes the bright white underside of its tail as an alarm signal when it bounds away.

C020.fun_fact: Red foxes can hear a mouse rustling underground and leap high to pounce straight down through grass or snow.

C022.fun_fact: The woodchuck (groundhog) is a true hibernator, sleeping so deeply through winter that its heartbeat slows to just a few beats a minute.

C023.fun_fact: A raccoon's dexterous paws get even more sensitive when wet, which is why it often appears to 'wash' its garden-raided food before eating.

C024.fun_fact: The Barred Owl's hooting sounds remarkably like a spoken phrase, a classic voice of New England's wooded edges at dusk.
C024.call: Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?

C027.fun_fact: Despite their bulk, black bears are excellent tree climbers and can sprint over 30 mph, and they're now common across much of Massachusetts.

C028.fun_fact: The bobcat is named for its short 'bobbed' tail, and this elusive cat lives throughout New England yet is rarely seen by people.

C029.fun_fact: American Goldfinches are strict vegetarians that nest late in summer so they can feed their young the thistle and seed they love.

C030.fun_fact: The Downy is North America's smallest woodpecker, a frequent backyard visitor that drums on branches to claim territory rather than to find food.

C031.fun_fact: Nearly all domestic duck breeds descend from the wild Mallard, and only the female gives the loud, classic 'quack.'

C039.fun_fact: The giant Polyphemus moth has no working mouthparts as an adult and never eats, living only about a week to find a mate.

C040.fun_fact: Giant pandas eat bamboo almost exclusively and have a 'pseudo-thumb,' an enlarged wrist bone that helps them grip stalks.

C041.fun_fact: Flamingos aren't born pink; their feathers turn rosy from pigments in the algae and tiny crustaceans they eat.

C042.fun_fact: Galapagos tortoises are among the longest-lived animals on land, with some individuals living well over a century.

C043.fun_fact: The male Resplendent Quetzal grows shimmering tail streamers that can be nearly three feet long, twice its body length.

C044.fun_fact: Every Bengal tiger's stripe pattern is unique, like a fingerprint, and the stripes mark the skin as well as the fur.

C045.fun_fact: A snow leopard's enormously thick tail can be nearly as long as its body and doubles as a warm wrap in the cold high mountains.

C046.fun_fact: The Tufted Titmouse hoards seeds for winter and will even pluck hair from live animals to line its nest.

C047.fun_fact: American Crows are remarkably intelligent, able to recognize individual human faces and remember them for years.

C048.fun_fact: The Red-bellied Woodpecker is named for a faint reddish wash on its belly, though its bright red cap is what people usually notice.

C049.fun_fact: The Mourning Dove's mournful song is often mistaken for an owl, and its wings whistle audibly when it bursts into flight.

C050.fun_fact: Blue Jays aren't actually blue; their feathers are brown, and the blue we see is a trick of light scattering in their structure.

C051.fun_fact: The White-breasted Nuthatch walks headfirst down tree trunks, a trick that lets it spot insects other birds miss.

C052.fun_fact: Eastern Gray Squirrels bury far more nuts than they recover, and the forgotten caches help plant New England's oak and hickory trees.

C053.fun_fact: A skunk's spray can reach about 10 feet, but it would rather stamp its front feet and warn you first.

C054.fun_fact: The green frog's call sounds like a loose banjo string being plucked near the garden pond.

C055.fun_fact: A single American toad can eat thousands of insects in a season, making it a gardener's quiet pest-control ally.

C056.fun_fact: This lungless salamander breathes entirely through its skin and is one of New England's most abundant forest vertebrates.

C057.fun_fact: Wild turkeys can sprint over 12 mph and burst into flight, despite Ben Franklin praising them as respectable birds.

C058.fun_fact: Ravens are among the smartest birds, using tools, mimicking sounds, and even playing by sliding down snowbanks.

C059.fun_fact: The woodcock performs a spiraling sky-dance at dusk and bobs its body in a comical rocking walk while probing for worms.

C060.fun_fact: Juncos are nicknamed snowbirds because these tidy gray-and-white sparrows arrive in New England as winter sets in.

C061.fun_fact: The hairy woodpecker looks like a larger twin of the downy, with a noticeably longer, chisel-like bill.

C062.fun_fact: Sapsuckers drill neat rows of small wells in trees, then return to sip the leaking sap and the insects it traps.

C063.fun_fact: The crow-sized pileated woodpecker chisels rectangular holes so big they can topple weakened trees.

C064.fun_fact: North America's only marsupial, the opossum can eat thousands of ticks and is largely resistant to rabies.

C065.fun_fact: A single big brown bat can devour hundreds of beetles and mosquitoes in one night over the garden.

C066.fun_fact: This mole's powerful, outward-turned hands dig tunnels so fast it can tunnel several feet in an hour.

C067.fun_fact: A porcupine can't shoot its quills, but its roughly 30,000 barbed quills detach easily on contact.

C068.fun_fact: The wide-eyed deer mouse is a key food source for owls and foxes, and an agile climber and jumper.

C069.fun_fact: Meadow voles carve tidy runways through grass and can have several litters a season, fueling local hawks and foxes.

C070.fun_fact: A snapping turtle can live decades, and on land its long neck strikes surprisingly fast when it feels cornered.

C071.fun_fact: For its tiny size, the spring peeper's chorus is astonishingly loud and is one of New England's first sounds of spring.

C072.fun_fact: The milk snake is a harmless rodent-eater that earned its name from an old myth that it milked cows in barns.

C073.fun_fact: Though often mistaken for a venomous cottonmouth, the northern water snake is harmless and hunts fish and frogs.

C074.fun_fact: Canada Geese mate for life and often return to the very pond where they hatched to raise their own goslings.

C075.fun_fact: The Great Horned Owl is one of the few predators that regularly eats skunks, seemingly unbothered by the spray.

C076.fun_fact: The Indigo Bunting isn't truly blue—its feathers have no blue pigment, and the dazzling color comes entirely from light refracting off their structure.

C077.fun_fact: The brilliant red male Scarlet Tanager molts to olive-green for winter, swapping his showy summer suit for camouflage.

C078.fun_fact: Cedar Waxwings are so fond of fruit they sometimes get tipsy on overripe, fermented berries.

C079.fun_fact: You can lure Baltimore Orioles to the garden with orange halves and grape jelly, which they adore.

C080.fun_fact: North America's smallest falcon, the American Kestrel can hover in place and even see ultraviolet trails of vole urine while hunting.

C081.fun_fact: The Peregrine Falcon is the fastest animal on Earth, diving at over 200 miles per hour to strike prey in midair.

C082.fun_fact: Cooper's Hawks are agile songbird-hunters that learned to thrive in towns, often staking out backyard bird feeders.

C083.fun_fact: Despite its name, the Ring-necked Duck is far easier to identify by the bold white ring around its bill than the faint neck ring.

C084.fun_fact: The Willow Flycatcher looks nearly identical to its cousins, so birders identify it mainly by its sneezy song.

C085.fun_fact: In spring, the male Ruffed Grouse drums a hollow thumping by beating his wings against the air, a sound you feel as much as hear.

C086.fun_fact: The Yellow-billed Cuckoo is a gardener's friend, one of the few birds that readily devours hairy, spiny tent caterpillars.

C087.fun_fact: The Ovenbird builds a domed, oven-shaped nest on the forest floor, complete with a side entrance.

C088.fun_fact: The Eastern Racer lives up to its name as one of our fastest snakes, and it hunts with its head raised to peer over the grass.

C089.fun_fact: A Bald Eagle's nest is among the largest of any bird, growing over the years into a structure that can weigh a ton.

C090.fun_fact: The Gray Fox is one of the only canids that can climb trees, scaling trunks with hooked claws to escape danger or reach fruit.

C091.fun_fact: Beavers' orange front teeth never stop growing, and the iron in the enamel makes them tough enough to fell whole trees.

C092.fun_fact: The American Mink is a superb swimmer with partly webbed feet, hunting both on land and underwater.

C093.fun_fact: The Long-tailed Weasel turns white in northern winters, swapping its brown coat for snowy camouflage.

C094.fun_fact: A single Little Brown Bat can snap up hundreds of mosquitoes and other insects in a single hour of nighttime hunting.

C095.fun_fact: The summer tanager is a bee and wasp specialist, catching them in flight and wiping the stingers off on a branch before eating.

C096.fun_fact: This shy boreal flycatcher nests on or near the ground in mossy spruce bogs, unusual for a flycatcher.

C097.fun_fact: The sky-blue cerulean warbler forages so high in the forest canopy that birders nickname its neck strain 'warbler neck.'

C098.fun_fact: In its courtship dive the male nighthawk pulls up sharply so air rushing through his wings makes a deep booming 'voom.'
C098.call: a nasal, buzzy 'peent' given in flight

C099.fun_fact: Red-headed woodpeckers are skilled flycatchers and one of the few woodpeckers that store food, wedging insects and nuts into bark crevices.

C100.fun_fact: This sparrow is named for its song, a thin, dry, insect-like buzz that really does sound like a grasshopper.

C101.fun_fact: The black-billed cuckoo is one of the few birds that gorges on hairy tent caterpillars, shedding its spine-lined stomach lining when it gets too matted.

C102.fun_fact: The orange-crowned warbler's namesake orange crown is usually hidden, flashing only when the bird is excited or displaying.

C103.fun_fact: The merlin is a compact, fast falcon that hunts by powering down small birds in level flight rather than diving on them.

C104.fun_fact: In the East, purple martins nest almost entirely in human-supplied housing, a tradition reaching back to Indigenous peoples who hung hollow gourds for them.

C105.fun_fact: The orchard oriole is North America's smallest oriole, and males wear a deep chestnut instead of the usual oriole orange.

C106.fun_fact: A bull moose grows and sheds a fresh set of antlers every year, regrowing the massive rack in a single summer.

C107.fun_fact: The fisher is one of the few predators that regularly hunts porcupines, flipping them to attack the unquilled face.

C108.fun_fact: The American ermine turns from brown to pure white in winter, keeping only a black tail tip year-round.

C109.fun_fact: The eastern red bat roosts alone in tree foliage, hanging by one foot so it looks just like a dead leaf.

C110.fun_fact: The snowshoe hare swaps its brown summer coat for white in winter and grows oversized, furry hind feet that act like snowshoes.

C111.fun_fact: The star-nosed mole's 22 pink tentacles let it identify and eat prey in under a quarter second, the fastest forager ever recorded.

C112.fun_fact: The eastern wood-pewee sings its lazy, drawn-out name from a high perch, often at dawn and dusk when other birds fall quiet.

C113.fun_fact: The eastern phoebe wags its tail constantly and was the first banded bird in North America, marked by Audubon to prove birds return to the same nest site.

C114.fun_fact: The veery's song spirals downward in an ethereal, flute-like cascade, produced using both sides of its voicebox at once.

C115.fun_fact: The hermit thrush is the only brown thrush that winters in the Northeast and is celebrated for its clear, flute-like opening note.
C115.call: an ethereal, flute-like song opening with one clear held note

C116.fun_fact: This tiny warbler builds its nest tucked inside hanging clumps of beard lichen or Spanish moss, almost never anywhere else.

C117.fun_fact: Its blue-gray head and bold white 'spectacles' around the eyes make it one of the easiest vireos to recognize in a New England forest.

C118.fun_fact: Despite its name it rarely screeches, instead giving a soft descending whinny or an even monotone trill, and comes in both gray and rusty-red color forms.
C118.call: a descending horse-like whinny and a soft monotone trill

C119.fun_fact: Blue Jays are notorious for imitating this hawk's screaming 'kee-aah' call, often to scatter other birds from a feeder.

C120.fun_fact: This frog can freeze nearly solid in winter, its heart stopping for weeks, then thaw out alive in spring thanks to natural antifreeze in its blood.

C121.fun_fact: The bright orange red eft is the land-roaming teenage stage of the eastern newt, wandering the forest floor for years before returning to water as a greenish adult.

C122.fun_fact: North America's only mildly poisonous native frog, it secretes skin toxins that make it distasteful to many predators.

C123.fun_fact: Males and females look so different - he's crisp blue, black and white, she's plain olive - that early naturalists mistook them for two separate species.

C124.fun_fact: One of the smallest owls in the East, it's named for a call said to sound like a saw being sharpened on a whetstone.

C125.fun_fact: This nocturnal bird is so devoted to its name-song that it can repeat the phrase hundreds of times in a row without pausing.

C126.fun_fact: Surprisingly clever, wood turtles have solved maze tests in the lab and will stomp their feet on the ground to coax earthworms to the surface.

C127.fun_fact: This gentle, slender snake is bright grass-green, eats mostly insects and spiders, and almost never bites - making it a true friend to the garden.

C128.fun_fact: On the first warm rainy nights of spring, these big black-and-yellow salamanders migrate en masse to breeding pools in an event known as 'Big Night.'

C129.fun_fact: This wide-eyed nocturnal squirrel doesn't truly fly - it glides between trees on a furred membrane, and many can glow faintly pink under ultraviolet light.

C130.fun_fact: A giant pale-green silk moth with long trailing tails, the adult has no mouth and never eats, living only about a week to find a mate.

C131.fun_fact: The largest native moth in North America, the cecropia can span six inches, yet the adult lives only a week or two and never feeds.

C132.fun_fact: Named for the spiky cogwheel crest on its back, this fierce predator hunts garden pests but can deliver a painful jab if handled, so admire it hands-off.

C133.fun_fact: Males sing a bubbling, banjo-like jumble of notes over hayfields, then migrate roughly 12,000 miles round-trip to South America and back each year.

C134.fun_fact: Not a true lark but a member of the blackbird family, the male flashes a bright yellow breast with a black 'V' and sings a clear, slurred whistle from a fencepost.

C135.fun_fact: One of North America's most threatened songbirds, it hybridizes readily with the blue-winged warbler, blurring the line between the two species.

C136.fun_fact: The largest and most powerful of the woodland accipiters, this fierce gray raptor will boldly defend its nest, sometimes diving at intruders who wander too close.

C137.fun_fact: This flycatcher perches atop dead snags and sallies out for insects, singing a whistled phrase often described as 'quick, three beers!'

C138.fun_fact: This tiny bat hibernates in caves and was pushed to federally endangered status by white-nose syndrome, a fungal disease that devastated its colonies.

C139.fun_fact: Named for its tricolored fur, this small bat is one of the first to emerge at dusk and has been hit hard by white-nose syndrome.

C140.fun_fact: New England's only native cottontail rabbit, it needs dense young-forest thickets and has dwindled to a fraction of its former range.

C141.fun_fact: This turtle's bright yellow throat and gentle smile are unmistakable, and it can live over 70 years, often traveling far overland between wetlands.

C142.fun_fact: Unlike most salamanders, this boldly banded species lays its eggs on land in autumn, with the female guarding them until rains flood the nest.

C143.fun_fact: This fuzzy bumblebee with a rusty smudge on its back was once common but is now federally endangered, the first U.S. bee to earn that status.

C144.fun_fact: This iridescent, lightning-fast predatory beetle sprints down sandy beaches after prey and is so rare it's federally threatened.

C145.fun_fact: This small, dusky-blue butterfly depends entirely on wild lupine and indigo, and its vanishing habitat has made it a protected species in many states.

C146.fun_fact: The most familiar bumblebee in eastern gardens, it 'buzz-pollinates' tomatoes and blueberries by vibrating flowers to shake pollen loose.

C147.fun_fact: Often mistaken for bumblebees, the males can't sting at all and the females rarely do, while both are busy pollinators of spring blooms.

C148.fun_fact: Paper wasps build their open, umbrella-shaped nests from chewed wood pulp and patrol your garden hunting caterpillars to feed their young.

C149.fun_fact: This harmless fly mimics a bee for protection, sipping nectar as an adult while its larvae devour garden-pest aphids by the hundreds.

C150.fun_fact: Despite the name, this is actually a large wasp that builds a football-shaped paper nest and helps control flies and other garden pests.

C151.fun_fact: This gentle, solitary wasp sculpts little tubes of mud for its nest and rarely stings, while hunting spiders to stock its nursery.

C152.fun_fact: This striking orange-legged solitary wasp is a calm pollinator that paralyzes katydids and crickets to provision its underground burrows.

C153.fun_fact: This solitary bee snips neat circles from leaves to line its nest and is such an efficient pollinator that it's farmed for alfalfa crops.

C154.fun_fact: A garden snail can retract entirely into its spiral shell and seal the opening with dried mucus to wait out dry spells for months.

L001.fun_fact: This sleek, tree-climbing weasel relative is a nimble forest hunter prized for its rich brown fur.
L001.lore: The American marten was trapped out and lost its old-growth forest across much of New England by the early 1900s, though it survives elsewhere and is slowly returning.

L002.fun_fact: A wolf of the northeastern woods, it hunted deer and beaver in family packs that shaped the whole ecosystem.
L002.lore: The eastern wolf was hunted, trapped, and poisoned out of New England by the late 1800s; debate continues over whether it is a distinct species or wolf-coyote lineage.

L003.fun_fact: Once the most abundant bird in North America, its migrating flocks darkened the sky for hours and could number in the billions.
L003.lore: The passenger pigeon was hunted relentlessly into oblivion; the last wild birds vanished by the 1900s and Martha, the final survivor, died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914.

L004.fun_fact: The heath hen was a coastal grouse whose males boomed and danced on communal 'booming grounds' each spring to court females.
L004.lore: Once common from New England to Virginia, the heath hen dwindled to a final flock on Martha's Vineyard; the last bird, 'Booming Ben,' died there in 1932.

L005.fun_fact: Wild turkeys can run up to 25 mph and roost in trees at night, and males fan their tails and gobble to draw a crowd of hens.
L005.lore: Overhunting and forest clearing wiped Massachusetts' wild turkeys out by the mid-1800s; the gobblers seen today descend from birds reintroduced in the 1970s.

L006.fun_fact: The eastern elk was a towering subspecies whose bugling bulls grew massive antlers and roamed forests and meadows in large herds.
L006.lore: Hunting and habitat loss erased the eastern elk from its range by the late 1800s; it was declared extinct, with the last animals gone around 1880.

L007.fun_fact: Woodland caribou grow hollow hair for insulation and broad, splayed hooves that work like snowshoes across deep snow and bog.
L007.lore: Logging, hunting, and warming winters pushed caribou out of New England; they vanished from the region by the early 1900s, surviving only far to the north.

L008.fun_fact: Wild Atlantic salmon hatch in rivers, journey thousands of miles to sea, then navigate back to spawn in the very stream where they were born.
L008.lore: Dams, pollution, and overfishing destroyed New England's wild salmon runs; the self-sustaining native populations were effectively lost by the late 20th century.

L009.fun_fact: The sea mink was the largest known mink, a coastal animal of the rocky New England and Maritime shoreline that hunted among the tide pools.
L009.lore: Prized by fur trappers, the sea mink was hunted relentlessly along the coast and driven to extinction in the late 1800s, around 1894.

L010.fun_fact: The great auk was a flightless North Atlantic seabird that 'flew' underwater with its wings, chasing fish like a northern penguin.
L010.lore: Hunted for feathers, eggs, and oil, the great auk's last confirmed pair was killed on Iceland's Eldey island in 1844.

L011.fun_fact: The Labrador duck was a sea duck with an oddly fringed, sensitive bill suited to sifting tiny shellfish from sandy coastal shallows.
L011.lore: Never abundant and poorly understood, the Labrador duck disappeared rapidly; the last one was recorded around 1875, one of the first known post-Columbian North American bird extinctions.

L012.fun_fact: The Eskimo curlew migrated in vast flocks between the Arctic and South America, one of the longest journeys of any New World shorebird.
L012.lore: Market hunting and prairie habitat loss collapsed its flocks by the early 1900s; with no confirmed sighting in decades, it is considered likely extinct.

L013.fun_fact: The Carolina parakeet was the only parrot native to the United States, a green-and-yellow bird that traveled in noisy, social flocks.
L013.lore: Killed as a crop pest and for its feathers, it dwindled to nothing; the last captive bird, 'Incas,' died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1918.

Y001.fun_fact: Cougars are remarkably wide-ranging cats, and a single young male documented traveling from the Midwest to Connecticut in 2011 covered over 1,500 miles.
Y001.lore: The eastern cougar was declared extinct by U.S. Fish & Wildlife (proposed 2011, finalized 2018), yet sightings of a 'big cat' are still reported across the Northeast.

Y002.fun_fact: Melanistic (all-black) bobcats are genuinely real but extraordinarily rare, with only a small handful ever documented, most from Florida.
Y002.lore: An all-black bobcat is occasionally reported in New England woods, but verified melanistic bobcats are so few that any local sighting remains unconfirmed.

Y003.fun_fact: The wolverine is the largest land-dwelling weasel, strong enough to drive larger predators off a kill and able to travel huge distances over snow.
Y003.lore: Wolverines are not resident in New England, so reports here are told as tales of a rare lone wanderer far from its northern range.

Y004.fun_fact: White gray squirrels are usually leucistic, with reduced pigment but normal dark eyes, and a few towns are famous for their thriving white colonies.
Y004.lore: Pale squirrels are reported here and there, and some communities so prize their rare white populations that the squirrels become local mascots.

Y005.fun_fact: Lake Champlain is one of the largest freshwater lakes in the U.S., deep and cold enough to fuel over a century of monster lore.
Y005.lore: Legend says 'Champ,' America's answer to Loch Ness, lurks in Lake Champlain; sightings have been reported on the Vermont-New York lake since the 1800s.

Y006.fun_fact: Pukwudgies appear in Wampanoag and wider Algonquian folklore as small, knee-high beings tied to the forests of southeastern New England.
Y006.lore: In Wampanoag legend the Pukwudgie is a mischievous, sometimes dangerous little forest spirit, said to haunt Massachusetts' Bridgewater Triangle.

Y007.fun_fact: The Dover Demon is one of New England's most famous one-night cryptid cases, known only from a cluster of teenage eyewitness reports.
Y007.lore: Legend holds that over two nights in 1977, teens in Dover, Massachusetts, reported a small, big-headed, big-eyed creature glimpsed along roadsides.

Y008.fun_fact: The Glawackus is a classic regional 'panic beast,' a creature whose description shifted with each retelling of the scare.
Y008.lore: Legend says a fierce, growling beast prowled Glastonbury, Connecticut, in 1939, spawning newspaper headlines, posses, and the nickname 'Glawackus.'

Y009.fun_fact: The 1817 Gloucester sea serpent reports were so numerous and detailed that a scientific society formally collected sworn eyewitness affidavits.
Y009.lore: In 1817, dozens reportedly saw a long, humped sea serpent in the harbor off Gloucester and Cape Ann, Massachusetts, fueling one of America's great sea-monster legends.

Y010.fun_fact: The Pioneer Valley's red sandstone is world-famous for dinosaur tracks, which 1800s Amherst scientist Edward Hitchcock believed were left by giant ancient birds.
Y010.lore: House legend says the Visitor is that track-maker still abroad: a tall, three-toed fog-walker with eyes like wet river stones who wanders the Connecticut River bottoms at dawn, paying calls on tobacco fields and gardens and leaving behind a single muddy footprint and a faint smell of river mud and crushed mint.

Y011.fun_fact: Lake Memphremagog is a long, deep glacial lake straddling the Vermont-Quebec border, the kind of cold, murky water that breeds monster lore.
Y011.lore: Legend says 'Memphre,' a serpentine lake creature, surfaces in Lake Memphremagog on the Vermont-Quebec border, with sightings reported for generations.
